The Banking Act of 1933, known by the names of its sponsors Senator Carter Glass and Representative Henry Steagall, was passed on 16 June 1933 as part of the New Deal. It answered the thousands of bank failures after the 1929 crash and the Great Depression.

It did two main things. It created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, insuring small savings accounts and so ending runs on banks. And it separated commercial banking (taking deposits and making loans) from investment banking (trading and underwriting stocks and bonds), forcing banks such as National City to give up one or the other. The Pecora hearings had shown how banks had pushed risky securities on depositors.

Parts of the separation were weakened over the years, and the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act removed it. After the 2008 financial crisis there were debates about bringing it back.

A Roosevelt law of 1933, it is one of the core pieces of modern US financial regulation.
